prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.1, 1 pt.)* Construct (draw) a directed graph with vertices $\{A,B,C,D\}$ and edges $\{(D\to A),(B\to C),(C\to A),(C\to D),(B\to A)\}$.
answer: The directed graph with these five edges.

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body: Draw the four vertices $A,B,C,D$ and the five arrows $D\to A$, $B\to C$, $C\to A$, $C\to D$, $B\to A$. This graph is almost a tournament: the only pair of players without an edge is $\{B,D\}$.

prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.2, 1 pt.)* A tournament is a directed graph with exactly one directed edge between every pair of distinct players. Redraw the graph with vertices $\{A,B,C,D\}$ and edges $\{D\to A,\ B\to C,\ C\to A,\ C\to D,\ B\to A\}$ and modify it to make it a tournament. (There are multiple possible constructions.)

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body: The only pair with no edge is $\{B,D\}$ (all other pairs $AB,AC,AD,BC,CD$ are already joined). Adding either $B\to D$ or $D\to B$ gives a tournament.

prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.3, 2 pt.)* Compute the number of different tournaments with $n$ players. Two tournaments are different if they have different outcomes for at least one game.

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body:
There are $\binom n2$ games, each with $2$ possible outcomes independently, so there are $2^{\binom n2}$ tournaments.

**Answer: $2^{n(n-1)/2}$**

prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.4, 1 pt.)* A tournament is *transitive* if whenever $p\to q$ and $q\to r$ (for distinct players) we also have $p\to r$. Construct a transitive tournament with $4$ players.
answer: E.g. $A\to B,A\to C,A\to D,B\to C,B\to D,C\to D$.

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body: Let $A$ beat $B,C,D$; $B$ beat $C,D$; $C$ beat $D$. If $p\to q$ and $q\to r$, then $p$ is earlier in the order $A,B,C,D$ than $q$, which is earlier than $r$, so $p\to r$.

prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.5, 4 pt.)* A tournament is a directed graph with exactly one edge between each pair of players. It is *transitive* if whenever $p,q,r$ are distinct with $p\to q$ and $q\to r$, then $p\to r$. How many different tournaments with $n$ players are transitive? Justify your answer.

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body:
Define $p>q$ iff $p\to q$. For a transitive tournament this relation is a strict total order on the players: any two distinct players are comparable (exactly one of $p\to q$, $q\to p$), and it is transitive (if $p\to q\to r$ then $p\ne r$, because $p\to q$ and $q\to p$ cannot both hold, so transitivity of the tournament gives $p\to r$). Conversely, every strict total order on the players defines a transitive tournament. So transitive tournaments correspond bijectively to rankings (orders) of the $n$ players, and there are $n!$ of them.

**Answer: $n!$**

prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.6, 2 pt.)* Seagulls love transitivity and will flip the results of some games in a tournament to make it transitive. Flipping a game replaces the edge $(p\to q)$ with $(q\to p)$. They are lazy, so they flip the fewest games possible. The tournament in the picture just occurred. Compute the number of games the seagulls will flip to make it transitive. (Also list the games they flip; there may be several correct answers.)

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body:
The tournament has the edge-disjoint cycles $B\to C\to D\to B$ and $C\to F\to E\to C$. A transitive tournament has no cycle (Problem 1.8), and each flip destroys at most one of two edge-disjoint cycles, so at least $2$ flips are needed.

Two flips suffice: flip $(D\to B)$ together with one of $(C\to F)$, $(E\to C)$ or $(F\to E)$. For example after flipping $D\to B$ and $C\to F$ the tournament is transitive (it is acyclic; a ranking is $B,F,E,C,D,A$ in which every player beats everyone below). A check of all rankings confirms that $2$ is the minimum.

**Answer: 2 flips, e.g. $(D\to B)$ and $(C\to F)$**

prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.7, 3 pt.)* A tournament is *acyclic* if for every player $p$ there is no sequence of edges starting at $p$ that ends at $p$. A tournament is *transitive* if whenever $p,q,r$ are distinct players with $p\to q$ and $q\to r$, we also have $p\to r$ (a tournament with 1 or 2 players is always transitive). Prove that if a tournament with $n\ge2$ players is acyclic, then it is transitive.
answer: Acyclic implies transitive: a violation would give a 3-cycle.

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body: A tournament with $2$ players is transitive. Let $n\ge3$ and suppose $p\to q$ and $q\to r$ for distinct players $p,q,r$. Since it is a tournament, either $p\to r$ or $r\to p$. If $r\to p$, then $p\to q\to r\to p$ is a sequence of edges from $p$ back to $p$, contradicting acyclicity. Hence $p\to r$, so the tournament is transitive. ∎

prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.8, 3 pt.)* A tournament is *acyclic* if for every player $p$ there is no sequence of edges starting at $p$ that ends at $p$. A tournament is *transitive* if whenever $p,q,r$ are distinct players with $p\to q$ and $q\to r$, we also have $p\to r$ (a tournament with 1 or 2 players is always transitive). Prove that if a tournament with $n\ge2$ players is transitive, then it is acyclic.

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body: Suppose a transitive tournament has a directed cycle $p_1\to p_2\to\cdots\to p_k\to p_1$ with $k\ge2$ distinct players (a closed walk contains such a cycle; $k=2$ is impossible since only one of $p_1\to p_2$, $p_2\to p_1$ exists, so $k\ge3$). By transitivity, $p_1\to p_2$ and $p_2\to p_3$ give $p_1\to p_3$; then $p_1\to p_3$ and $p_3\to p_4$ give $p_1\to p_4$, and so on, until $p_1\to p_k$. But $p_k\to p_1$ is an edge, and a tournament cannot contain both $p_1\to p_k$ and $p_k\to p_1$, a contradiction. ∎

prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.9, 7 pt.)* Seagulls flip the fewest number of games necessary to make a tournament transitive (flipping $p\to q$ turns it into $q\to p$). Another tournament with $6$ players takes place, and it turns out to be the worst case: no tournament on $6$ players would require more flips. How many games do the seagulls need to flip in this worst case? Prove that no tournament with $6$ players ever requires more than this number of flips and that there exists a tournament where this many flips are needed.

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body:
**Answer 4.** A tournament is transitive iff it is acyclic (Problems 1.7, 1.8), so we want the minimum number of edges to reverse to destroy all cycles.

**Lower bound (a tournament needing 4 flips).** Label the players $1,\dots,6$ and let the $15$ games be $1\to5,1\to6,2\to1,2\to4,2\to6,3\to1,3\to2,4\to1,4\to3,5\to2,5\to3,5\to4,6\to3,6\to4,6\to5$). It contains the four edge-disjoint $3$-cycles $1\to5\to3\to1$, $1\to6\to4\to1$, $2\to4\to3\to2$, $2\to6\to5\to2$. Each flip removes at most one of these edge-disjoint cycles, and a transitive tournament has no cycles, so at least $4$ flips are needed. (A computer search over all rankings also gives exactly $4$ for this tournament.)

**Upper bound.** *Claim 1.* Let $v$ be a player of an $n$-tournament $T$ with score $s_v$. If $T-v$ can be made transitive with $m$ flips, then $T$ can be made transitive with at most $\min(n-1-s_v,\ s_v)+m$ flips. Indeed, flip the $n-1-s_v$ edges into $v$ (so $v$ beats everyone) or the $s_v$ edges out of $v$ (so $v$ loses to everyone); these do not involve $T-v$, so we may also make $T-v$ transitive with $m$ flips. The result is transitive: a triple $x\to y\to z$ not containing $v$ is fine; if $v$ beats everyone, a triple containing $v$ with $x\to y\to z$ must have $x=v$ and then $v\to z$; if $v$ loses to everyone, it must have $z=v$ and $x\to v$.

*Claim 2.* A $3$- or $4$-tournament needs at most $1$ flip. A $3$-tournament is transitive or a $3$-cycle, and flipping one edge of a $3$-cycle makes it transitive. For a $4$-tournament the scores sum to $6$. If some player has score $3$ or $0$, Claim 1 (with $m\le1$) gives at most $0+1=1$ flip. Otherwise all scores are $1$ or $2$: the score sequence is $(1,1,2,2)$. Let $a\to b$ be the two players of score $2$; $b$ beats both players of score $1$ while $a$ beats exactly one of them, $c$, and loses to the other, $d$; since $d$ has one win already, $c\to d$. Flipping $d\to a$ makes $a$ beat everyone, $b$ beat $c,d$ and $c$ beat $d$: transitive.

*Claim 3.* A $5$-tournament needs at most $3$ flips, and at most $2$ unless its scores are $(2,2,2,2,2)$. The scores sum to $10$, so the maximum score $m\ge2$ with $m=2$ only for $(2,2,2,2,2)$. Apply Claim 1 to a player of score $m$ (flipping the $4-m$ edges into it) together with Claim 2: at most $(4-m)+1=5-m$ flips, i.e. $\le2$ if $m\ge3$ and $\le3$ if $m=2$.

*The 6-tournament.* The scores sum to $15$, so the maximum score is at least $3$.
- If some player $v$ has score $4$ or $5$: flip the $5-s_v\le1$ edges into $v$, then Claim 3: at most $1+3=4$ flips.
- If the maximum score is $3$, the score sequence is $(0,3,3,3,3,3)$, $(1,2,3,3,3,3)$ or $(2,2,2,3,3,3)$. In the first two, take $v$ of smallest score $s_v\le1$ and flip the $s_v$ edges out of $v$, then Claim 3: at most $1+3=4$. In the last, among the three players of score $2$ the three games produce three wins, so one of them, $v$, wins at most one of its two games against the others and loses to another score-$2$ player $u$. Flip the $2$ edges out of $v$. In $T-v$ the player $u$ (who beat $v$) has score $1$, so the scores of $T-v$ are not $(2,2,2,2,2)$ and Claim 3 gives at most $2$ more flips: total $\le4$.

So $4$ flips always suffice, and $4$ are needed for the tournament above. **Answer: 4** ∎

prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.10, 5 pt.)* A *cycle* of length $k$ in a tournament is a sequence of distinct players $p_1\to p_2\to\cdots\to p_k\to p_1$. A tournament is transitive iff it is acyclic (Problems 1.7, 1.8). Prove that if a tournament has a cycle of length $k$, where $k\ge3$, then it has a cycle of length $i$ for every $3\le i\le k$.
answer: Standard pancyclicity: build a 3-cycle, then extend one vertex at a time.

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body:
Let $C_0$ be a cycle of length $k$ and let $T'$ be the subtournament on its $k$ players; $T'$ is strongly connected (every player reaches every other along $C_0$).

**A 3-cycle exists.** $T'$ is not acyclic, hence by Problem 1.7 it is not transitive: there are distinct $x,y,z$ with $x\to y\to z$ but not $x\to z$, i.e. $z\to x$. So $x\to y\to z\to x$ is a $3$-cycle.

**Extending.** Suppose $T'$ has a cycle $C=u_1\to u_2\to\dots\to u_i\to u_1$ with $3\le i<k$. We show it has a cycle of length $i+1$. Let $x$ be a player of $T'$ not on $C$. If for some $j$ we have $u_j\to x$ and $x\to u_{j+1}$ (indices mod $i$), insert $x$ between $u_j$ and $u_{j+1}$ to get length $i+1$. Otherwise each outside player $x$ satisfies: if $u_j\to x$ then $u_{j+1}\to x$, so going around the cycle either every $u_j$ beats $x$ or none does. Let $A$ be the set of outside players beaten by all of $C$, and $B$ the set of outside players that beat all of $C$. Both are nonempty and there is an edge from $A$ to $B$: since $T'$ is strongly connected and $C\ne T'$, a path from $C$ to an outside player leaves $C$ through an edge $u_j\to x$, so $A\neq\emptyset$; similarly a path from outside into $C$ enters through some $y\to u_j$, so $B\ne\emptyset$. Take a path from some $a\in A$ to some player of $B$ and look at the first vertex on it that is not in $A$: it cannot be in $C$ (as $C\to A$), so it is in $B$, and the vertex before it is in $A$. Hence there are $a\in A$, $b\in B$ with $a\to b$. Then $u_1\to a\to b\to u_3\to u_4\to\dots\to u_i\to u_1$ is a cycle of length $(i-1)+2=i+1$ (it uses $u_1\to a$ because $C\to A$, and $b\to u_3$ because $B\to C$; for $i=3$ read $u_3=u_i$).

Starting from the $3$-cycle and repeating, we get cycles of every length $3,4,\dots,k$. ∎

prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.11, 2 pt.)* A tournament is a directed graph with exactly one edge between each pair of players; it is transitive if $p\to q$ and $q\to r$ always imply $p\to r$ (for distinct $p,q,r$). A *subtournament* keeps a subset of the players with all results between them. Prove that any tournament with $2^2=4$ players contains a transitive subtournament with $3$ players.
answer: Take a player with at least 2 wins.

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body: In a $4$-player tournament there are $6$ games, so the four scores sum to $6$ and some player $p$ has at least $2$ wins (otherwise the sum is at most $4$). Let $p\to q$ and $p\to r$. Whichever of $q\to r$ or $r\to q$ holds, the players $p,q,r$ form a transitive subtournament ($p$ beats both, and the other game is consistent). ∎

prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.12, 6 pt.)* A tournament is a directed graph with exactly one edge between each pair of players; it is transitive if $p\to q$ and $q\to r$ always imply $p\to r$ (for distinct $p,q,r$). A *subtournament* keeps a subset of the players with all the results between them. Prove that for every positive integer $n$, any tournament with $2^n$ players contains a transitive subtournament with $n+1$ players.
answer: Induction on n using pigeonhole on winners/losers of one player.

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body: Induction on $n$. For $n=1$, a tournament with $2$ players is transitive and has $n+1=2$ players. Suppose the claim holds for $n=k$ and consider a tournament with $2^{k+1}$ players. Pick any player $u$; the other $2^{k+1}-1$ players split into the set $W$ of players that beat $u$ and the set $L$ of players that lose to $u$. By pigeonhole one of them has at least $2^k$ players, so it contains a transitive subtournament $S$ with $k+1$ players. If it lies in $L$, add $u$ as the top player of $S$ ($u$ beats everyone in $S$); if it lies in $W$, add $u$ as the bottom player (everyone in $S$ beats $u$). In both cases the result is a transitive subtournament with $k+2$ players. ∎

prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.1, 1 pt.)* The *score* of a player is the number of games the player wins (outgoing edges); the *score sequence* lists the scores in nondecreasing order. Compute the score sequence for the tournament in the picture.

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body:
Reading the arrows: $B\to C,A,E$; $C\to D,A,E$; $D\to B,A$; $E\to D,A$; and $A$ beats nobody. The scores are $A:0$, $D:2$, $E:2$, $B:3$, $C:3$, so the score sequence is $(0,2,2,3,3)$.

**Answer: $(0,2,2,3,3)$**

prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.2, 2 pt.)* The *score* of a player is the number of games the player wins (outgoing edges); the *score sequence* lists the scores in nondecreasing order. A tournament is *transitive* if whenever $p,q,r$ are distinct players with $p\to q$ and $q\to r$, we also have $p\to r$ (a tournament with 1 or 2 players is always transitive). Find all possible score sequences for a transitive tournament with $n$ players. Justify your answer.

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body:
A transitive tournament is a strict total order (Problem 1.5): list the players $q_1,\dots,q_n$ from best to worst; then $q_i$ beats exactly $q_{i+1},\dots,q_n$, so $q_i$ has score $n-i$. The only score sequence is $(0,1,2,\dots,n-1)$.

**Answer: $(0,1,\dots,n-1)$**

prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.3, 1 pt.)* A tournament is *reducible* if its players can be partitioned into two nonempty sets $W$ and $L$ such that every player in $W$ beats every player in $L$; otherwise it is *irreducible*. Construct a tournament with $5$ players that is reducible into a group of $3$ and a group of $2$. List the two sets of players and label them "winners" and "losers".

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body: Take players $A,B,C,D,E$ with $A\to B\to C\to A$, $D\to E$, and each of $D,E$ beating each of $A,B,C$. The winners are $W=\{D,E\}$ and the losers $L=\{A,B,C\}$; every player of $W$ beats every player of $L$.

prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.4, 1 pt.)* A *random* $n$-tournament is a tournament in which, for every pair of players $(p,q)$ independently, the probability that $p$ beats $q$ is $\frac12$. A tournament is *reducible* if its players can be partitioned into two nonempty sets $W,L$ with every player of $W$ beating every player of $L$. Compute the probability that a random $3$-tournament is reducible.

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body:
There are $2^3=8$ equally likely tournaments on $3$ players. Two are $3$-cycles, which are irreducible (no player beats both others). The other $6$ are transitive: the top player beats the other two, so $W=\{\text{top}\}$, $L=\{\text{the others}\}$ shows they are reducible. The probability is $\frac68=\frac34$.

**Answer: $\frac34$**

prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.5, 5 pt.)* The *score* of a player is the number of games the player wins (outgoing edges); the *score sequence* lists the scores in nondecreasing order. A tournament is *reducible* if its players can be partitioned into two nonempty sets $W$ and $L$ such that every player in $W$ beats every player in $L$; otherwise it is *irreducible*. Prove that if the absolute difference between the scores of any two players of an $n$-tournament $T_n$ is less than $\frac n2$, then $T_n$ is irreducible.
answer: Reducible forces a score gap of at least n/2.

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body:
Suppose $T_n$ is reducible with $W,L$ as in the definition, $|L|=k$ and $|W|=n-k$, where $1\le k\le n-1$. Players of $L$ lose to all of $W$, so their wins are only against other players of $L$: the total score of $L$ is $\binom k2$, and some $\ell\in L$ has score at most $\frac{k-1}2$. Players of $W$ each beat all $k$ players of $L$, and the games inside $W$ give a further total of $\binom{n-k}2$ wins, so some $w\in W$ has score at least $k+\frac{n-k-1}2$. Then
$$s_w-s_\ell\ \ge\ k+\frac{n-k-1}{2}-\frac{k-1}{2}=\frac n2,$$
contradicting the hypothesis that all score differences are less than $\frac n2$. Hence $T_n$ is irreducible. ∎

prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.6, 2 pt.)* A tournament is *reducible* if its players can be partitioned into two nonempty sets $W$ and $L$ such that every player in $W$ beats every player in $L$; otherwise it is *irreducible*. Prove that every irreducible tournament with $4$ players contains a cycle of length $3$ (that is, $x\to y\to z\to x$ for some players $x,y,z$).

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body: Suppose a tournament has no $3$-cycle. If $p\to q$ and $q\to r$ for distinct players, then $r\to p$ would be a $3$-cycle, so $p\to r$: the tournament is transitive, hence a strict total order, and its top player $w$ beats everyone else. Then $W=\{w\}$ and $L=$ all other players is a valid partition, so the tournament is reducible. Therefore an irreducible tournament must contain a $3$-cycle. ∎

prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.7, 3 pt.)* A tournament is *reducible* if its players can be partitioned into two nonempty sets $W$ and $L$ such that every player in $W$ beats every player in $L$; otherwise it is *irreducible*. Prove that every irreducible tournament with $n\ge4$ players contains a cycle of length $3$ (that is, $x\to y\to z\to x$ for some players $x,y,z$).

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body: We prove the contrapositive: a tournament with at least $2$ players and no $3$-cycle is reducible. If $p\to q\to r$ (distinct), then $r\to p$ would be a $3$-cycle, so $p\to r$; thus the tournament is transitive, i.e. a strict total order (Problem 1.5). Its top player $w$ beats every other player, so $W=\{w\}$, $L=V\setminus\{w\}$ is a valid partition. Hence irreducible tournaments contain a $3$-cycle. ∎

prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.8, 2 pt.)* A *Hamiltonian path* in a tournament is an ordering $(p_1,\dots,p_n)$ of all the players with $p_1\to p_2\to\cdots\to p_n$. A tournament is transitive if $p\to q$ and $q\to r$ always imply $p\to r$ (for distinct players). Prove that every transitive tournament has a Hamiltonian path.

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body: A transitive tournament is a strict total order on its players (Problem 1.5). List the players from best to worst, $p_1,\dots,p_n$; each $p_i$ beats every later player, in particular $p_i\to p_{i+1}$. So $p_1\to p_2\to\cdots\to p_n$ is a Hamiltonian path. ∎

prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.9 (a), 4 pt.)* A *directed path* joining distinct players $p_1,\dots,p_i$ of a tournament is a sequence of edges $p_1\to p_2\to\cdots\to p_i$. Suppose you have a nonempty directed path joining $p_1,\dots,p_i$ and a player $x$ not already on the path. Prove that you can always create a directed path joining $p_1,\dots,p_i$ and $x$ (in some order).
answer: Insert x at the front, the back, or between two consecutive players.

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body: If $x\to p_1$, put $x$ first: $x\to p_1\to\cdots\to p_i$. Otherwise $p_1\to x$. If $p_i\to x$, put $x$ last. Otherwise $x\to p_i$. Let $j$ be the largest index with $p_j\to x$; then $1\le j<i$, and since $p_{j+1}\not\to x$ we have $x\to p_{j+1}$. So $p_1\to\cdots\to p_j\to x\to p_{j+1}\to\cdots\to p_i$ is a directed path through all of them. ∎

prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.9 (b), 1 pt.)* A *Hamiltonian path* in a tournament is a directed path $p_1\to p_2\to\cdots\to p_n$ through all players. Prove that every tournament has a Hamiltonian path. (You may use the fact that a directed path joining some players can always be extended to include any outside player $x$, in some order.)
answer: Add players one at a time.

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body: Start with a path consisting of a single player and add the remaining players one at a time; by the extension fact each step produces a directed path through all players added so far. After $n$ steps we have a Hamiltonian path. ∎

prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.10, 2 pt.)* The *score* of a player is the number of games the player wins (outgoing edges); the *score sequence* lists the scores in nondecreasing order. A score sequence is *valid* if some tournament has exactly these scores. Are the following score sequences valid? (1) $(1,1,2,2)$; (2) $(1,1,3,3,3,4)$; (3) $(3,3,3,3,3,3,3)$; (4) $(1,1,1,2,4,6,6)$. For valid sequences no justification is needed; for invalid ones give a brief explanation. Give your answer as four words valid / not valid.

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body:
(1) Valid: players $1,\dots,4$ with $1\to4$, $2\to1$, $3\to1$, $3\to2$, $4\to2$, $4\to3$ have scores $1,1,2,2$.

(2) Valid: players $1,\dots,6$ with the games $2\to1$, $1\to3$, $4\to1$, $1\to5$, $1\to6$, $3\to2$, $4\to2$, $5\to2$, $6\to2$, $4\to3$, $5\to3$, $6\to3$, $5\to4$, $6\to4$, $6\to5$ have scores $3,1,1,3,3,4$ (a permutation of $(1,1,3,3,3,4)$).

(3) Valid: players $0,\dots,6$ (mod $7$) with $i\to i+1,\,i+2,\,i+3$; every player wins exactly $3$ games.

(4) Not valid: the four players with the smallest scores play $\binom42=6$ games among themselves, each giving a win to one of these four players, so their scores must total at least $6$; but $1+1+1+2=5<6$.

**Answer: valid, valid, valid, not valid**

prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.11, 2 pt.)* The *score* of a player is the number of games the player wins (outgoing edges); the *score sequence* lists the scores in nondecreasing order. Let $S=(s_1\le\dots\le s_n)$ be the score sequence of a tournament. Prove that $\sum_{i=1}^ks_i\ge\binom k2=\frac{k(k-1)}2$ for all $1\le k\le n$, with equality at $k=n$.
answer: Each game among k players gives a win to one of them.

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body: The $k$ players with the smallest scores play $\binom k2$ games among themselves, and each such game gives one win to one of these $k$ players. So their total score is at least $\binom k2$. For $k=n$ every game is among the $n$ players and gives exactly one win, so the total is exactly $\binom n2$. ∎

prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.12, 12 pt.)* The *score* of a player is the number of games the player wins (outgoing edges); the *score sequence* lists the scores in nondecreasing order. Let $S=(s_1\le\dots\le s_n)$ be a nondecreasing sequence of integers with $\sum_{i=1}^ks_i\ge\binom k2=\frac{k(k-1)}2$ for all $1\le k\le n$, with equality at $k=n$. Prove that $S$ is a valid score sequence, i.e. that some tournament has scores exactly $s_1,\dots,s_n$.

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body:
(*Landau's theorem.*) The condition holds for every set of indices: for any $X$ with $|X|=k$, $\sum_{i\in X}s_i\ge s_1+\dots+s_k\ge\binom k2$ since $S$ is sorted.

We must orient each edge of the complete graph $K_n$ towards its loser so that vertex $i$ is the tail of exactly $s_i$ edges. Build a bipartite graph: on the left, one node for each of the $\binom n2$ games $e=\{i,j\}$; on the right, $s_i$ copies of each vertex $i$; join the node $e=\{i,j\}$ to all copies of $i$ and all copies of $j$. A matching that saturates the left side assigns every game to one of its two players (the winner), with at most $s_i$ games assigned to $i$.

Hall's condition: take a set $F$ of games and let $X$ be the set of players involved, $|X|=k$. The neighbours of $F$ are the copies of the vertices of $X$, which number $\sum_{i\in X}s_i\ge\binom k2\ge|F|$ (there are at most $\binom k2$ games among $k$ players). By Hall's theorem there is a matching saturating all $\binom n2$ games. Since the right side has $\sum s_i=\binom n2$ nodes, every copy is used, so vertex $i$ wins exactly $s_i$ games. This is a tournament with score sequence $S$. ∎

prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 3.1, 1 pt.)* A player $k$ is a *king* if $k$ beats every other player, or for every player $m$ that beats $k$ there is a player $p$ with $k\to p$ and $p\to m$. A king that beats all other players is *Alexandrian*. Draw a $3$-tournament with exactly $1$ king and another with exactly $3$ kings.

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body:
*Exactly one king:* the transitive tournament $A\to B$, $A\to C$, $B\to C$. $A$ beats everyone, so $A$ is a king. $B$ loses to $A$ and would need $B\to p\to A$, but nobody beats $A$; so $B$ is not a king. $C$ beats nobody, so it is not a king.

*Exactly three kings:* the cycle $A\to B\to C\to A$. Each player beats one player and loses to the other, which is beaten by the one it beats (e.g. $A\to B\to C$ reaches $C$ in two steps), so all three are kings.

prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 3.2, 2 pt.)* A player $k$ is a *king* if $k$ beats every other player, or for every player $m$ that beats $k$ there is a player $p$ with $k\to p$ and $p\to m$. A king that beats all other players is *Alexandrian*. Show that no $4$-tournament can have exactly $2$ kings.
answer: Casework on a player with score 3, score 0, otherwise (1,1,2,2).

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body:
The scores of a $4$-tournament sum to $6$.

- If some player $a$ has score $3$ ($a$ beats everyone), then $a$ is a king and no other player $x$ is: $x$ loses to $a$ and nobody beats $a$, so $x$ cannot reach $a$ in two steps. Exactly $1$ king.
- If some player $z$ has score $0$, then $z$ beats nobody, so $z$ cannot reach anyone and is not a king. A player $x\ne z$ beats $z$ directly, and $z$ is no use as an intermediate vertex (it beats nobody), so $x$ is a king of $T$ iff it is a king of the $3$-tournament on the others. A $3$-tournament has $1$ king (transitive) or $3$ kings (cycle) by Problem 3.1. So $T$ has $1$ or $3$ kings.
- Otherwise all scores are $1$ or $2$, so the scores are $(1,1,2,2)$. Let $a\to b$ be the two players of score $2$; $b$ beats both players of score $1$, and $a$ beats exactly one of them, say $c$, and loses to $d$ (so $d\to a$); $d$ already has a win, hence $c\to d$. Then $a$ is a king ($a\to c\to d$ reaches $d$), $b$ is a king ($b\to d\to a$), $d$ is a king ($d\to a\to b$ and $d\to a\to c$), but $c$ is not: $b$ beats $c$ and $c\to u\to b$ is impossible ($c$ beats only $d$, and $d\not\to b$). Exactly $3$ kings.

In all cases the number of kings is $1$ or $3$, never $2$. ∎

prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 3.3 (a), 2 pt.)* A player $k$ is a *king* if $k$ beats every other player, or for every player $m$ that beats $k$ there is a player $p$ with $k\to p$ and $p\to m$. A king that beats all other players is *Alexandrian*. For a player $p$ let $W^p$ be the set of players that $p$ beats and $L^p$ the set of players that beat $p$; $\mathcal W_p$ and $\mathcal L_p$ denote the subtournaments on these sets (a *subtournament* keeps all the results of games between the chosen players). (King Seagull Theorem.) Suppose a player $k$ has the most wins in the tournament, or is tied for the most wins, and suppose for contradiction that $k$ is not a king, i.e. there is a player $p$ such that $k$ does not reach $p$ in one or two steps. Argue that $p$ must beat everyone in the subtournament $\mathcal W_k$ (and also beats $k$).
answer: If $k$ does not reach $p$ in 2 steps, p beats all of $W^k$.

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body: Since $k$ does not beat $p$ in one step, $p\to k$. For any $w\in W^k$ (so $k\to w$): if $w\to p$ then $k\to w\to p$ would reach $p$ in two steps, contrary to assumption. Hence $p\to w$ for every $w\in W^k$: $p$ beats everyone in $\mathcal W_k$. ∎

prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 3.3 (b), 3 pt.)* A player $k$ is a *king* if $k$ beats every other player, or for every player $m$ that beats $k$ there is a player $p$ with $k\to p$ and $p\to m$. A king that beats all other players is *Alexandrian*. For a player $p$ let $W^p$ be the set of players that $p$ beats and $L^p$ the set of players that beat $p$; $\mathcal W_p$ and $\mathcal L_p$ denote the subtournaments on these sets (a *subtournament* keeps all the results of games between the chosen players). Let $k$ be a player with the most wins (possibly tied). Show that $|W^p|>|W^k|$ if $p$ is a player as in 3.3(a) (that is, $p\to k$ and $p$ beats everyone in $W^k$), and use this to prove that every tournament has at least one king.

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body: If $p\to k$ and $p$ beats everyone in $W^k$, then $W^p\supseteq W^k\cup\{k\}$ and $k\notin W^k$, so $|W^p|\ge|W^k|+1>|W^k|$, contradicting that $k$ has the most wins. Therefore no such $p$ exists, i.e. $k$ reaches every player in one or two steps, so $k$ is a king. Thus a player with the most wins is always a king, and every tournament has at least one king. ∎

prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 3.4 (a), 1 pt.)* A player $k$ is a *king* if $k$ beats every other player, or for every player $m$ that beats $k$ there is a player $p$ with $k\to p$ and $p\to m$. A king that beats all other players is *Alexandrian*. For a player $p$ let $W^p$ be the set of players that $p$ beats and $L^p$ the set of players that beat $p$; $\mathcal W_p$ and $\mathcal L_p$ denote the subtournaments on these sets (a *subtournament* keeps all the results of games between the chosen players). Every tournament has at least one king. Let $T$ be a tournament and $p$ a player that has lost to at least one other player. Explain why the nonempty subtournament $\mathcal L_p$ contains a king (of $\mathcal L_p$).
answer: Apply the existence of a king to the tournament L_p.

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body: $L^p$ is nonempty and $\mathcal L_p$ is itself a tournament; every tournament has a king (a player with the most wins in it), so $\mathcal L_p$ has a king. ∎

prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 3.4 (b), 2 pt.)* A player $k$ is a *king* if $k$ beats every other player, or for every player $m$ that beats $k$ there is a player $p$ with $k\to p$ and $p\to m$. A king that beats all other players is *Alexandrian*. For a player $p$ let $W^p$ be the set of players that $p$ beats and $L^p$ the set of players that beat $p$; $\mathcal W_p$ and $\mathcal L_p$ denote the subtournaments on these sets (a *subtournament* keeps all the results of games between the chosen players). Argue that any king of $\mathcal L_p$ is also a king of $T$.
answer: Cases for the player m: in L^p, equal to p, or in W^p.

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body:
Let $k$ be a king of $\mathcal L_p$; so $k\in L^p$, i.e. $k\to p$. Take any player $m\ne k$ of $T$.
- If $m\in L^p$, then $k$ reaches $m$ in one or two steps inside $\mathcal L_p$ (as $k$ is a king of $\mathcal L_p$).
- If $m=p$, then $k\to p$ directly.
- If $m\in W^p$ (so $p\to m$), then $k\to p\to m$ reaches $m$ in two steps.
Thus $k$ reaches every other player in at most two steps, so $k$ is a king of $T$. ∎

prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 3.5, 1 pt.)* A player $k$ is a *king* if $k$ beats every other player, or for every player $m$ that beats $k$ there is a player $p$ with $k\to p$ and $p\to m$. A king that beats all other players is *Alexandrian*. Construct a $4$-tournament in which some player has at least one win but is not a king.

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body: Take the transitive tournament in which $A$ beats $B,C,D$, $B$ beats $C,D$, and $C$ beats $D$. Player $B$ has wins ($B\to C$, $B\to D$) but loses to $A$, and nobody beats $A$, so $B$ cannot reach $A$ in two steps: $B$ is not a king.

prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 3.6, 3 pt.)* A player $k$ is a *king* if $k$ beats every other player, or for every player $m$ that beats $k$ there is a player $p$ with $k\to p$ and $p\to m$. A king that beats all other players is *Alexandrian*. Show that a king is unique if and only if it is an Alexandrian king. (Show both directions: any unique king is Alexandrian, and any Alexandrian king is the unique king.)
answer: Use that someone who lost has lost to a king.

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body:
($\Leftarrow$) Let $a$ be an Alexandrian king (it beats every other player). Any other player $x$ loses to $a$, and nobody beats $a$, so $x$ cannot reach $a$ in one or two steps; $x$ is not a king. So $a$ is the unique king.

($\Rightarrow$) Let $k$ be the unique king and suppose some player $p$ beats $k$. Then $k$ has lost, so $\mathcal L_k$ is nonempty and contains a king $q$ of $\mathcal L_k$ which is a king of $T$ (Problems 3.4(a),(b)). Since $q\in L^k$, $q\ne k$, a second king, a contradiction. So nobody beats $k$: $k$ beats everyone, i.e. $k$ is Alexandrian. ∎

prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 3.7, 3 pt.)* A player $k$ is a *king* if $k$ beats every other player, or for every player $m$ that beats $k$ there is a player $p$ with $k\to p$ and $p\to m$. A king that beats all other players is *Alexandrian*. Prove that no tournament can have exactly $2$ kings.
answer: If k1 beats k2, use that someone who lost has lost to a king.

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body: Suppose a tournament has exactly two kings $k_1,k_2$, and say $k_1\to k_2$. If nobody beat $k_1$, then $k_1$ would be an Alexandrian king, hence the unique king (Problem 3.6), contradiction. So $k_1$ lost to someone, and $\mathcal L_{k_1}$ contains a king of $T$ (Problems 3.4(a),(b)) which beats $k_1$. This king is different from $k_1$ so it is $k_2$, and $k_2\to k_1$, contradicting $k_1\to k_2$. ∎

prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 3.8, 2 pt.)* A tournament is *random* if each game is won by either player with probability $\frac12$ independently. A player is an *Alexandrian king* if it beats all other players. Show that the probability that a random $n$-tournament contains an Alexandrian king approaches $0$ as $n\to\infty$. (You may use that $p(n)/q(n)\to0$ if $p$ is a polynomial and $q$ an exponential with base greater than $1$.)

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body: A fixed player beats all $n-1$ others with probability $2^{-(n-1)}$. By the union bound, the probability that some player is an Alexandrian king is at most $n\cdot2^{-(n-1)}=\frac{2n}{2^n}\to0$. ∎

prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 3.9, 1 pt.)* A pair of players $(p,q)$ is *non-dominating* if $p$ loses against $q$ and, for every player $r$ that $q$ loses to ($r\in L^q$), $p$ loses against $r$. Let $S$ be the $3$-tournament on $\{p_1,p_2,p_3\}$ with edges $p_1\to p_2$, $p_1\to p_3$, $p_2\to p_3$. Identify all non-dominating pairs in $S$.

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body:
The pairs $(p,q)$ with $p$ losing to $q$ are $(p_2,p_1)$, $(p_3,p_1)$, $(p_3,p_2)$. For $(p_2,p_1)$ and $(p_3,p_1)$: $p_1$ loses to nobody, so $L^{p_1}=\emptyset$ and the condition holds vacuously. For $(p_3,p_2)$: $L^{p_2}=\{p_1\}$ and $p_3$ loses to $p_1$. So all three are non-dominating.

**Answer: $(p_2,p_1),\ (p_3,p_1),\ (p_3,p_2)$**

prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 3.10, 1 pt.)* A pair of players $(p,q)$ is *non-dominating* if $p$ loses against $q$ and, for every player $r$ that $q$ loses to ($r\in L^q$), $p$ loses against $r$. Identify all non-dominating pairs in the cyclic tournament $S'$ on $\{q_1,q_2,q_3\}$ with edges $q_1\to q_2$, $q_2\to q_3$, $q_3\to q_1$.

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body:
The pairs $(p,q)$ with $p$ losing to $q$ are $(q_2,q_1)$, $(q_3,q_2)$, $(q_1,q_3)$. For $(q_2,q_1)$: $L^{q_1}=\{q_3\}$ and $q_2$ beats $q_3$, so the condition fails; by symmetry the same happens for the other two pairs. There are no non-dominating pairs.

**Answer: none**

prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 3.11, 3 pt.)* In a random $n$-tournament (each game is won by either player with probability $\frac12$, independently), a pair $(p,q)$ is *non-dominating* if $p$ loses against $q$ and, for every player $r$ that $q$ loses to, $p$ loses against $r$. For an ordered pair of distinct players $(p,q)$, find the probability that $(p,q)$ is non-dominating.

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body:
We need $q\to p$ (probability $\frac12$). For each of the other $n-2$ players $r$ (independently), the bad event is "$r\to q$ but $p\to r$" (then $r\in L^q$ and $p$ does not lose to $r$), which has probability $\frac14$; so the condition holds for $r$ with probability $\frac34$. These events involve disjoint games for different $r$. The probability is $\frac12\left(\frac34\right)^{n-2}$.

**Answer: $\frac12\left(\frac34\right)^{n-2}$**

prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 3.12, 3 pt.)* A player $k$ is a *king* if $k$ beats every other player, or for every player $m$ that beats $k$ there is a player $p$ with $k\to p$ and $p\to m$. A king that beats all other players is *Alexandrian*. A pair $(p,q)$ is *non-dominating* if $p$ loses to $q$ and loses to every player that $q$ loses to. In a random $n$-tournament each pair $(p,q)$ is non-dominating with probability $\frac12\left(\frac34\right)^{n-2}$. Use this to give a lower bound on the probability that every player of a random $n$-tournament is a king. Your bound should approach $1$ as $n\to\infty$.

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body:
If $p$ is not a king, there is a player $q$ with $q\to p$ such that no $r$ with $p\to r$ has $r\to q$; equivalently, every $r\in L^q$ satisfies $r\to p$, which says exactly that $(p,q)$ is non-dominating. So if some player is not a king, some ordered pair is non-dominating. By the union bound over the $n(n-1)$ ordered pairs, $P(\text{some pair is non-dominating})\le n(n-1)\cdot\frac12\left(\frac34\right)^{n-2}$. Hence
$$P(\text{every player is a king})\ \ge\ 1-\frac{n(n-1)}2\left(\frac34\right)^{n-2},$$
which tends to $1$ as $n\to\infty$ since a polynomial times $\left(\frac34\right)^n$ tends to $0$. ∎

prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 3.13, 2 pt.)* A player $k$ is a *king* if $k$ beats every other player, or for every player $m$ that beats $k$ there is a player $p$ with $k\to p$ and $p\to m$. A king that beats all other players is *Alexandrian*. For a player $p$ let $W^p$ be the set of players that $p$ beats and $L^p$ the set of players that beat $p$; $\mathcal W_p$ and $\mathcal L_p$ denote the subtournaments on these sets (a *subtournament* keeps all the results of games between the chosen players). A tournament $T$ is *super-kingable* if there is a tournament $X$ containing $T$ as a subtournament such that the set of kings of $X$ is exactly the set of players of $T$. Prove that if a non-trivial tournament $T$ (more than one player) is super-kingable, then $T$ itself has no Alexandrian king.
answer: Use that a king of L^a is a king of X.

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body: Suppose $T$ has at least $2$ players, $X\supseteq T$ has exactly the players of $T$ as kings, and $a$ is an Alexandrian king of $T$. Then $a$ is a king of $X$. If nobody in $X$ beat $a$, then $a$ would be Alexandrian in $X$, hence the unique king of $X$ (Problem 3.6), but $X$ has at least two kings (the players of $T$). So some player beats $a$ and $\mathcal L_a$ in $X$ is nonempty; it contains a king of $\mathcal L_a$, which is a king of $X$ (Problems 3.4(a),(b)). Hence this player belongs to $T$. But every player of $T$ other than $a$ loses to $a$ (as $a$ is Alexandrian in $T$), so none of them lies in $L^a$, and $a\notin L^a$: a contradiction. ∎

prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 3.14, 6 pt.)* A player $k$ is a *king* if $k$ beats every other player, or for every player $m$ that beats $k$ there is a player $p$ with $k\to p$ and $p\to m$. A king that beats all other players is *Alexandrian*. A tournament $T$ is *super-kingable* if there is a tournament $X$ containing $T$ as a subtournament such that the set of kings of $X$ is exactly the set of players of $T$. Prove that if a non-trivial tournament $T$ (more than one player) contains no Alexandrian king, then $T$ is super-kingable.
answer: Add one new player y_x for each player x of T.

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body:
Let $V$ be the players of $T$, $|V|\ge2$. Since $T$ has no Alexandrian king, every $x\in V$ loses to some player of $T$; fix one such player $m_x\in V$ with $m_x\to x$.

**Construction.** Add a new player $y_x$ for every $x\in V$ with the results: $y_x\to x$; $v\to y_x$ for all $v\in V\setminus\{x\}$; and among the new players, $y_{m_x}\to y_x$ for every $x$ (these requirements are consistent: they would conflict only if $y_{m_x}\to y_x$ and $y_x\to y_{m_x}$ both were required, i.e. $m_x=m$ and $m_m=x$, which would need $m\to x$ and $x\to m$). All remaining games between new players are decided arbitrarily. Call the result $X$; $T$ is a subtournament of $X$.

**Every $v\in V$ is a king of $X$.** Let $m$ be a player that beats $v$.
- $m\in V$: then $v\to y_m$ (as $v\ne m$) and $y_m\to m$: two steps.
- $m=y_x$ with $x\ne v$: impossible since $v\to y_x$ for $x\ne v$.
- $m=y_v$: then $v\to y_{m_v}$ (since $m_v\ne v$) and $y_{m_v}\to y_v$: two steps.
So $v$ reaches every player that beats it within two steps; all other players it beats directly.

**No new player is a king.** Consider $y_x$ and the player $m_x\in V$. We have $m_x\to y_x$ (since $m_x\ne x$). Suppose $y_x\to u\to m_x$. The players $u$ that $y_x$ beats are $x$ and some new players. $u=x$ fails because $m_x\to x$, not $x\to m_x$. If $u=y_z$ is new, then $y_z\to m_x$ requires $z=m_x$ (new player $y_z$ beats only $z$ among $V$), so $u=y_{m_x}$; but $y_{m_x}\to y_x$ so $y_x\not\to y_{m_x}$. So $y_x$ cannot reach $m_x$ in two steps, and it is not a king.

Hence the kings of $X$ are exactly the players of $T$, and $T$ is super-kingable. ∎
